A fixed vocabulary is simpler as a table than as branching code
Recursive helper turning 0–999 into a list of words: hundreds, then the rest < 100, then the rest < 20
Breaking a number into smaller same-shaped pieces
Returns (quotient, remainder) in one call: how many of this unit, and what is left
Peeling off billions, millions, thousands in turn
Collects words in order and appends the scale name only if the chunk is nonzero

p: `1234567`. Each row peels one scale off the remainder:
bullets: Final string: `One Million Two Hundred Thirty Four Thousand Five Hundred Sixty Seven`.

blocks.h: Why a list of words and not string concatenation?
p: Building a list and joining at the end avoids stray spaces: empty groups simply add nothing, so there is no `strip()` cleanup. The `if chunk:` check handles values like 1,000,000, where the thousands group is zero and must not print 'Thousand'.

bullets: Time: O(1). The number has at most 10 digits, so the work is bounded.
Space: O(1).

p: `num == 0` is handled first because the loop would otherwise return an empty string. Teens (11–19) never reach `tens[...]`, which is why `ones` is extended to 19.

273.takeaway: Chunk by powers of 1000, convert each 0–999 piece with a small recursive helper, and join the nonempty words.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Number of colourings of the first i posts where the last two posts have the same colour
DP with a small number of states
Number of colourings where the last two posts differ
New `same` = old `diff` (copy the previous post's colour, only allowed if the one before differed). New `diff` = any previous colouring times (k − 1) other colours
Simultaneous assignment uses the old values on the right
Posts 3..n; posts 1 and 2 are the base case

p: `k = 2` colours. Row i gives the counts after painting i posts (`n = 3` gives 6, `n = 4` gives 10):

At most two adjacent posts may share a colour. Painting post i the same as post i−1 is allowed only if post i−1 differed from post i−2; otherwise three in a row would match. So `same(i) = diff(i−1)`. A new colour for post i can follow either state and has k − 1 choices, so `diff(i) = (same(i−1) + diff(i−1)) * (k − 1)`.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

p: `n == 1` returns k early because there is no 'previous post' to define `same` and `diff`; for n = 2 the loop is skipped and the answer is `k + k(k−1) = k²`.

276.takeaway: Paint Fence: track colourings ending in a matching pair vs a different pair; a matching pair can only extend a differing pair.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: `i` position in the digit string, `expr` the expression text so far, `val` its value, `last` the last term added (signed)
Backtracking that builds the answer and its value together
Takes `num[i..j]` as the next operand, so multi-digit numbers like 12 are tried
Operands with a leading zero (like '05') are illegal, but '0' alone is fine
Undoes the previous term and re-adds it multiplied: fixes precedence of `*` without an expression parser
Evaluating on the fly with a correction term
First operand has no operator in front of it

p: `num = "123"`, `target = 6`. Each row is a completed expression:

With `1+2*3` the multiplication must bind tighter than the earlier addition. When `*3` arrives, the code removes the last term (`val − last`, here 2) and adds back `last * n` (2·3). So `1 + 2` (val 3, last 2) becomes `3 − 2 + 6 = 7`, matching 1+2*3 = 7. For subtraction `last` is stored negated (`−n`) so a following `*` still scales the right sign.

bullets: Time: O(4ⁿ · n) at worst: each gap between digits has up to 4 choices (nothing, +, −, *), and building each string costs O(n).
Space: O(n) recursion plus the output.

282.takeaway: Backtrack over operator choices while keeping the running value and last term, so multiplication is applied by correcting the last term.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Best candidate so far: the smallest value greater than p seen on the way down
p.val < cur.val → succ = cur; cur = cur.left
cur is larger than p, so it is a candidate; a smaller candidate may be to the left
cur is too small (or is p itself), so the successor is to the right, if it exists
None if every step turned right (p is the maximum)

bullets: Returns `2`.

p: BST `[5,3,6,2,4,null,null,1]`, p = 6 (the largest value):
bullets: Every step goes right and `succ` stays `None`.

blocks.h: Why does remembering the last left-turn work?
p: The inorder successor is either the leftmost node of p's right subtree or, if p has no right subtree, the lowest ancestor for which p lies in the left subtree. The code never looks at p's own subtree. It just searches by value from the root, and `succ` ends up as the smallest value greater than `p.val`, which is what the successor means. Both cases are covered by the same rule.

bullets: Time: O(h) (O(log n) balanced, O(n) skewed).
Space: O(1). No parent pointers needed.

285.takeaway: BST successor by value: search from the root and remember the last node where you went left.

Set of strings already assigned, so two letters never map to the same string
Enforcing the reverse direction of a bijection
Checks whether `w` occurs in `s` starting exactly at index j, without slicing
Matching a known word at a position
Tries every possible length for a brand-new word
Undo the assignment when the branch fails

p: `pattern = "abab"`, `s = "redblueredblue"`. The search tries 7 fresh word assignments in total, most of them in failed branches, before the assignments below succeed:

head: pattern letter
word it stands for
remaining check
rows: s.startswith('blue', 10) → match, i and j both at the end → True

bullets: Result: `True`. Once `a` and `b` are mapped, repeated letters are verified with `startswith` in O(len(word)) without further branching.

p: Without it `a → red` and `b → red` would both be accepted, even though a bijection requires different letters to map to different strings. For `pattern = "ab"` and `s = "redred"` the answer must be False, and `used` is what rejects the split red + red.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Preorder write: value for a node, `#` marker for a missing child
Making the tree shape recoverable from a flat string
Joins tokens into one string / splits them back
Shared iterator: each `next` consumes the next token across recursive calls
Reading a sequence without passing indexes
Same order as the write: left subtree first, then right

bullets: `deserialize` reads the same string in the same order and rebuilds the tree: 1(2,3(4,5)) in `v(left,right)` form.

p: Preorder alone is ambiguous: `1,2,3` could be a chain or a root with two children. The `#` for each missing child makes every node's subtree end at a known place, so the recursion knows exactly when to return to the parent.

bullets: Time: O(n) for both directions.
Space: O(n) for the string and O(h) recursion.

297.takeaway: Serialize in preorder with null markers; deserialize with the same preorder recursion over a shared iterator.

Binary search: the first index where tails[i] ≥ x (insertion point), O(log n); `tails` stays sorted
Finding where a value fits in a sorted list
x is larger than every tail, so the longest subsequence grows
x is a smaller (or equal) ending for length i+1, which keeps more future options open
Length of the LIS (not the subsequence itself)

bullets: `tails` is not necessarily a real subsequence: for `[3,5,1]` it ends as `[1,5]`, although 5 comes before 1. Only its length is meaningful.

p: The problem wants a strictly increasing subsequence, so an equal value must replace its equal, not extend it.

head: x = 5, tails = [2, 5, 7]
result

The DP solution is O(n²) but easier to extend to reconstructing the sequence.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: From `itertools`: running totals, yielding nums[0], nums[0]+nums[1], …
Prepends 0 so that `pre[i]` is the sum of the first i elements; the empty prefix has sum 0
Avoids a special case when left = 0
Sum of nums[left..right] by subtracting two prefixes

blocks.h: Why is the extra 0 in front helpful?
p: Without it, `sumRange(0, r)` would need `pre[r] - pre[-1]`. Index −1 would wrap to the last element in Python and silently give a wrong answer. The leading zero shifts all indexes by one so that every query is the same subtraction.

bullets: Build: O(n). Each query: O(1).
Space: O(n) for the prefix array.
Works because the array is immutable; if updates were allowed, a Fenwick tree would be needed (problem 307).

303.takeaway: Prefix sums with a leading zero make any range sum a single subtraction.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Best profit while holding a stock at the end of the day
Best profit if the stock was sold today (so tomorrow must be a cooldown)
Best profit while holding nothing and free to buy
Saves yesterday's `sold` before it is overwritten
Needed because `rest` must see the old value
Buy today: only allowed from `rest`, not from `sold`
This is how the cooldown is enforced
Yesterday's sale becomes tradeable again today after the cooldown

p: `prices = [1,2,3,0,2]`. Values are the states at the end of each day:
bullets: Answer: `max(sold, rest) = 3` (buy 1, sell 3, cooldown, buy 0, sell 2).

p: Within one day, `sold` is recomputed first. `rest` must use the *previous* day's `sold`, because a sale today cannot be rebought today. Saving `prev_sold` before the update keeps the cooldown rule.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(1).

309.takeaway: Cooldown as a three-state machine (hold, sold, rest): buying is only possible from rest, which is reached one day after a sale.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Pads with virtual balloons of value 1 so the edge balloons also have two neighbours
Max coins from bursting every balloon strictly between l and r (l and r themselves stay)
Solves small intervals first so that `dp[l][k]` and `dp[k][r]` exist
max(… for k in range(l+1, r))
k is the LAST balloon burst inside (l, r)
Choosing the last item makes subproblems independent
When k is burst last, its neighbours are exactly l and r

p: `nums = [3,1,5,8]` → `a = [1,3,1,5,8,1]`. Table rows are intervals in the order they are computed:

blocks.h: Why choose the LAST balloon, not the first?
p: If you pick the first balloon to burst, its neighbours depend on everything else, and the two sides remain linked. If k is the last one burst in (l, r), then when it is burst only l and r remain beside it, and the two sides (l, k) and (k, r) have already been solved without influencing each other. That independence is what makes the DP work.

bullets: Time: O(n³): O(n²) intervals, each trying O(n) choices of k.
Space: O(n²).

312.takeaway: Burst Balloons is interval DP over the last balloon burst: dp[l][r] = max over k of dp[l][k] + dp[k][r] + a[l]·a[k]·a[r].

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Largest subsequence of length t from one array, using a monotonic stack that may drop `len − t` smaller earlier digits
while drop and st and st[-1] < x
A smaller digit before a bigger one is dropped while we still have drops left
If fewer drops happened than allowed, trims the tail
Greedy merge: take the front digit from the lexicographically larger list
List comparison is lexicographic, so ties between equal fronts are broken by looking at later digits
Lists compare lexicographically, equal lengths → numeric order

p: `nums1 = [3,4,6,5]`, `nums2 = [9,1,2,5,8,3]`, `k = 5`. For each split `i` (digits from nums1) and `k − i` (from nums2):

blocks.h: Why compare whole lists in `merge` instead of just the front digits?
p: With fronts equal, say `a = [6,7]` and `b = [6,0]`, taking from `a` first yields `6,7,6,0`; taking from `b` first yields `6,6,7,0`. Looking only at the front would tie and could pick the worse one. Comparing the remaining lists chooses the one whose future is larger.

bullets: Time: about O(k · (m + n + k²)): up to k + 1 splits; each does two picks in O(m + n) and a merge that costs O(k²) here because of `pop(0)` and the list comparisons.
Space: O(k).

321.takeaway: Split k across both arrays, take the best subsequence of each with a monotonic stack, merge greedily comparing whole remainders, and keep the max.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Size of the small half; the extra middle element goes to the small half for odd lengths
Smaller half, reversed (largest of the small half first)
Slice assignment: writes into the even positions 0, 2, 4, … in place

p: Duplicates are the danger. Take sorted `[1,2,2,2,3,3]`. Interleaving without reversing gives `[1,2,2,3,2,3]`, where `2,2` are adjacent and the required `<`/`>` pattern breaks. With both halves reversed the result is `[2,3,2,3,1,2]`, which satisfies it. Reversing keeps equal values from meeting across the boundary between the halves.

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort.
Space: O(n) for the sorted copy and slices.

324.takeaway: Wiggle Sort II: sort, then interleave the reversed lower half into even slots and the reversed upper half into odd slots.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Every integer in [1, reach] can already be formed as a subset sum
The next number leaves no gap: adding it extends the range to reach + nums[i]
Patching with the smallest missing number (reach + 1) doubles the range to 2·reach + 1
Greedy: the best patch is always the first gap

blocks.h: Why is the best patch always `reach + 1`?
p: The number `reach + 1` is the smallest value that cannot be formed. Any patch must be ≤ `reach + 1` to close that gap, and among those, the largest (`reach + 1` itself) extends the range most: new reach `2·reach + 1`. A smaller patch extends it less, so it can never need fewer patches.

bullets: Time: O(len(nums) + log n): each patch roughly doubles `reach`.
Space: O(1).
`nums` must be sorted (the problem guarantees it).

330.takeaway: Patching Array: keep the covered range [1, reach]; use the next number if it fits, otherwise patch reach + 1 to double it.

What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Dict word → index for O(1) lookup of a reversed piece
Replace an inner loop over all words with a hash lookup
Every split point of word w, including k = 0 and k = len(w)
Palindrome test by comparing with the reverse slice
Finds a word equal to the reverse of the leftover suffix, or None
If pre is a palindrome, the partner goes in front: partner + w. If suf is a palindrome, the partner goes after: w + partner
Skips the second case at k = len(w), where `suf` is empty and the pair would be duplicated

p: `words = ["abcd","dcba","lls","s","sssll"]`. Pairs found while scanning each word's splits:

blocks.h: Why only check splits where one side is a palindrome?
p: For `a + b` to be a palindrome, the longer word has a palindromic leftover once the shorter one's reverse is matched against it. So for each word, split it into a matched piece and a palindromic piece; the matched piece's reverse must exist as another word. This turns an O(n²) pair check into O(n·L) lookups.

bullets: Time: O(n · L²): n words, L+1 splits each, each split doing O(L) palindrome and reverse work.
Space: O(n · L) for the dict.

336.takeaway: Palindrome Pairs: for every split of every word, if one side is a palindrome, look up the reverse of the other side in a hash map.

blocks.h: Why pass depth as a parameter?
p: Depth is local to each call: going into a sublist adds one, and returning leaves the caller's depth unchanged. A global depth counter would need explicit increments and decrements around every recursive call.

bullets: Time: O(N), N = total number of elements at all levels.
Space: O(D) recursion for maximum depth D.

339.takeaway: Depth-weighted sum is a DFS that carries the current depth down: integer × depth, list → recurse with depth + 1.

Skipping irrelevant characters with two pointers

p: `"IceCreAm"`: the vowels are I, e, e, A. Swaps in order:

blocks.h: Why guard the inner whiles with `left < right`?
p: Without the guard, a string with no vowels (e.g. `"bcd"`) would run `left` past the end and raise IndexError. With it, the pointers meet and the outer loop ends; the final swap of an element with itself is harmless.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Net score per row and per column: +1 for player 1, −1 for player 2
Counting instead of storing the board
Net score on the two diagonals
Cell lies on the main diagonal
A line holding n marks of one player has net ±n; a mixed line cannot reach ±n

p: 3×3 board, moves in order. Columns show the counters after each move:

blocks.h: Why +1/−1 instead of two counters per line?
p: A single signed counter per line is enough: it reaches ±n only if all n cells belong to one player, because opposing marks cancel out. This halves the state and makes the win test a single `abs(...) == n`.

bullets: Time: O(1) per move, instead of O(n) for scanning a row/column/diagonal.
Space: O(n) for the row and column counters.

348.takeaway: Tic-Tac-Toe in O(1) per move: signed counters for each row, column and both diagonals.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Sort by width ascending, and for equal widths by height DESCENDING
Multi-key sort with a negated key
After sorting, widths are handled; only heights matter
Binary search insertion point (strictly increasing LIS)
Standard O(n log n) longest increasing subsequence on the heights

bullets: LIS of heights has length 3: (2,3) → (5,4) → (6,7).

blocks.h: Why sort equal widths by height descending?
p: Envelopes of the same width cannot nest. If equal widths were sorted by height ascending, the LIS on heights could pick both `(6,4)` and `(6,7)` as consecutive increasing heights. Sorting equal widths descending (`(6,7)` before `(6,4)`) means two same-width envelopes can never form an increasing pair, so the height-LIS is automatically valid. Ascending order here: [[6, 4], [6, 7]], descending: [[6, 7], [6, 4]].

bullets: Time: O(n log n) for the sort and the LIS.
Space: O(n).

354.takeaway: Russian Doll = LIS on heights after sorting by width ascending and height descending for ties.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: f = lambda x: a*x*x + b*x + c
Two pointers at the ends of the sorted input
The transformed values are largest (a>0) or smallest (a<0) at the ends
Fill the output from the back (largest first) for an upward parabola, from the front (smallest first) for a downward one
Whichever end maps to the larger value (a ≥ 0) is placed next

p: `nums = [-4,-2,2,4]`, `a=1, b=3, c=5` (upward parabola, so largest values are at the ends). Filling from the right:

`f` is a parabola, so over a sorted input the values form a valley (a > 0) or a hill (a < 0). The extremes of the transformed sequence are therefore at the two ends of the input, and moving inwards gives the next largest (or smallest) value. This replaces an O(n log n) sort with a merge-like O(n) pass. (If `a == 0`, f is linear and monotonic; the `a >= 0` branch still works because the larger end is always one of the two ends.)

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(n) for the output.

360.takeaway: Sort Transformed Array: a parabola's extremes are at the ends of the sorted input, so fill the output from the outside in with two pointers.

head: Code
What it does
Reach for it when
rows: Returns the node's height: distance to its farthest leaf (a leaf is 0, None is −1)
Height from the children, so children are processed first
Opens a new group the first time a height appears
Grow a list of buckets on demand
The node is removed in round h+1, together with every node of the same height

p: Tree `[1,2,3,4,5]`; nodes in the order the post-order DFS finishes them:

blocks.h: Why does height equal the removal round?
p: A node can only be removed after all of its descendants are gone, i.e. in the round after its tallest child subtree is removed. That round number is exactly the node's height (counting leaves as round 0). So grouping by height reproduces repeated leaf removal in a single traversal, with no tree mutation.

bullets: Time: O(n).
Space: O(h) recursion, plus the output.

366.takeaway: Find Leaves: group nodes by height (distance to the deepest leaf below) with one post-order traversal.
